summary: Describes a framework for keeping media confidential and intact end to end in switched conferencing, where the media distributors in the middle are not trusted with encryption keys. It builds on existing security mechanisms. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: In a group call, a server forwards everyone's video. This document shows how to seal the video so even the server passing it along cannot peek inside.

questions: how to make conferencing end to end encrypted

subtitle: How a group video call can keep its media secret from the very servers that forward it.

tldr.problem: In switched conferencing, a Media Distributor forwards everyone's media, but running it in a cloud the participants do not fully trust puts the privacy of that media at risk.
tldr.mechanism: Media is encrypted twice with SRTP: an inner end-to-end key that only trusted endpoints know, and an outer hop-by-hop key that the Media Distributor does use. A Key Distributor hands out the keying material and the Media Distributor never sees the end-to-end keys.
tldr.outcome: Media Distributors can still forward packets and adjust certain RTP headers, but cannot decrypt or undetectably alter the media. RTCP and RTP header extensions remain protected only hop by hop.

facts.label: Key types
facts.value: HBH key, E2E key, KEK (EKT Key)

facts.label: DTLS roles
facts.value: Endpoint is client; Key Distributor is server

facts.label: Example scale
facts.value: 1,000 participants means at least 1,000 distinct SRTP master keys

today: RFC 8871 is a Proposed Standard, published in January 2021, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the double transform in RFC 8723 and the EKT key transport in RFC 8870.

sections.title: Why Private Conferencing Needs a Framework
sections.content:
In switched conferencing, a Media Distributor does not mix, transcode or recompose the media. It simply forwards the flows from each participant to the others, often only a subset such as the active speakers. It may make limited changes to RTP headers, but the voice or video content is left unaltered.

This makes Media Distributors easy to run on general-purpose hardware, including virtualized public and private clouds. Those clouds have been viewed as less secure because the resources are not always physically controlled by those who use them. RFC 8871 defines a framework where a Media Distributor cannot get the keys needed to decrypt or authenticate the media, while still being able to modify certain RTP headers, add or change header extensions, and handle RTCP.

The framework reuses existing RTP security mechanisms with minimal enhancements. It does not try to hide the fact that a conference is taking place.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper server passes everybody's video around the group. This document makes sure the helper can pass it along without being able to peek at it.

sections.title: Trusted and Untrusted Entities
sections.content:
The framework splits the system into trusted and untrusted entities. "Untrusted" does not mean the entity is expected to misbehave. It means only that the entity has no access to the end-to-end (E2E) media encryption keys.

  • Media Distributor (untrusted): forwards RTP flows, authenticates each packet hop by hop, relays secured messages between endpoints and the Key Distributor, and gets per-hop key information from the Key Distributor.
  • Call processing (untrusted in the simple scenario): handles call signaling and may authenticate endpoints for joining the conference.
  • Endpoint (trusted): terminates the E2E encryption and holds E2E key information. Resistance to endpoint compromise is out of scope.
  • Key Distributor (trusted): gives key information to endpoints for both E2E and hop-by-hop (HBH) security, and to Media Distributors for HBH security.

Key Distributors MUST reject DTLS associations with any unauthorized endpoint or Media Distributor. Which parties are authorized is something the Key Distributor must know, but how it learns that is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Some helpers are allowed to hold the keys, like your friends. Others, like the mail carrier, only move the boxes around and never get a key.

sections.title: Two Layers of Encryption
sections.content:
The framework uses two security contexts with two keys. The "inner" key is a distinct E2E key for each transmitted media flow, used for authenticated encryption of RTP media between endpoints. The "outer" key is an HBH key known only to a Media Distributor and the adjacent endpoint (or peer Media Distributor) on that hop.

The double transform from RFC 8723 lets endpoints apply both contexts while keeping the usual SRTP interface. The Media Distributor just uses the normal single AES-GCM transform with the HBH keys.

Every packet MUST be authenticated hop by hop, and each HBH key is distinct per hop. Because endpoints can rebuild the original RTP header, they can still authenticate packets end to end, which leaves the Media Distributor free to change the header values allowed by RFC 8723. Replay protection as in RFC 3711 is REQUIRED at each hop.

RTCP and RTP header extensions are encrypted only hop by hop. Endpoints MUST NOT send confidential information in either.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note goes in a small locked box for your friends, and then that box goes in a bigger box for each stretch of the trip. The carrier opens only the big box.

sections.title: Keys and Key Exchange
sections.content:
PERC uses three kinds of key. The HBH key is an SRTP master key for hop-by-hop protection. The E2E key is the SRTP master key an endpoint uses to encrypt its own media. The KEK (the EKT Key from RFC 8870) is shared by all endpoints and encrypts each endpoint's E2E key so receivers can decrypt its media.

Each endpoint runs a DTLS-SRTP handshake with the Key Distributor, with the Media Distributor tunneling the packets. The endpoint MUST act as the DTLS client and the Key Distributor MUST act as the DTLS server, and the Key Distributor MUST authenticate the tunneling Media Distributor first. The handshake yields key material "double" the size needed: one half is for E2E, the other half becomes the HBH key, which the Key Distributor also passes to the Media Distributor. The KEK arrives in an EKTKey message.

An endpoint may use the DTLS-SRTP-derived E2E key or generate a fresh one, and MUST change it whenever the EKT Key changes. It sends its E2E key to others in a Full EKT Tag, encrypted under the KEK. All endpoints share one SRTP master salt, which comes from the Key Distributor. Even the Key Distributor does not know the locally generated E2E keys. Between two Media Distributors, the HBH key comes from DTLS-SRTP run directly between them.

The Key Distributor may rekey by sending a new EKTKey. Endpoints then create a new SRTP master key, use the EKT SPI field to tell old and new keys apart, and SHOULD keep old keys long enough to decrypt late or out-of-order packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in the group gets one secret handshake from a trusted keeper. Each person also makes their own personal lock and sends it to the group wrapped in the group handshake. The carrier never learns the handshake.

sections.title: Authenticating the Parties
sections.content:
Entities need to validate each other, especially the Key Distributor and endpoints. The critical requirements are that an endpoint can verify it is talking to the correct Key Distributor for the conference, and that the Key Distributor can verify the endpoint is the right one. The details are outside the scope of the document, but it describes two approaches.

With identity assertions, a WebRTC identity assertion (RFC 8827) binds the user's identity to the fingerprint of the DTLS-SRTP certificate, which is unique to a call and conference. This requires an Identity Provider trusted by the endpoints and the Key Distributor. With certificate fingerprints in session signaling, for example SIP and SDP carrying fingerprints, the fingerprint must be securely mapped to a user and delivered to the Key Distributor. The Key Distributor and Media Distributor also need endpoint-to-conference mappings, based on a conference-specific unique identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Before handing out keys, the keeper checks everyone's ID, and everyone checks that the keeper is the real one.

sections.title: The Encrypted Media Packet
sections.content:
Figure 4 of the RFC shows an RTP packet after the double transform, with an EKT Tag appended. The RTP header and payload are covered by both layers. The inner (E2E) layer adds an E2E authentication tag, then the outer (HBH) layer adds an OHB field and an HBH authentication tag. The EKT Tag is appended after the double transform and is neither encrypted nor authenticated.

The Media Distributor can therefore verify and re-protect the outer layer, while the inner authentication tag lets the receiving endpoint detect tampering.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet is like a letter in an envelope inside another envelope, with a sticker on the outside that is not sealed at all.

sections.title: Attacks the Framework Considers
sections.content:
Third parties on the path are limited by HBH integrity protection and encryption, and off-path attackers' crafted packets are dropped when HBH authentication fails. A fake Media Distributor can only cause denial of service, since it has neither HBH nor E2E keys.

A malicious Media Distributor cannot read or undetectably modify E2E-authenticated data. Dropping packets is not mitigated, though. Replay is addressed by replay protection, and E2E replay protection MUST be provided for the duration of the conference. Delayed playout is possible because receivers must accept gaps when a Media Distributor forwards only some streams. Periodic rekeying reduces its effect. Splicing is prevented because the SSRC is included in both the HBH and E2E integrity checks. Since RTCP has no E2E protection, a compromised Media Distributor can tamper with or forge RTCP messages such as picture requests.

The Key Distributor is a high-value target: access to its keying material would let an adversary decrypt media from any endpoint, even years later if packets were recorded. Endpoints are also trusted, and since all participants share the same KEK, a compromised endpoint could inject media with a new or another endpoint's SSRC. The suite defined for PERC only shows that the sender had received the KEK.
sections.plainLanguage: The carrier cannot read or change your notes without getting caught, but it could throw some away or deliver an old one late. The most important thing to guard is the keeper of the keys.

viz.caption: THE THREE KEY TYPES IN PERC

items.title: HBH key
items.text: SRTP master key for one hop; known to the Media Distributor and the adjacent endpoint.

items.title: E2E key
items.text: SRTP master key an endpoint uses to encrypt its own media; never given to a Media Distributor.

items.title: KEK (EKT Key)
items.text: Shared by all endpoints; encrypts each E2E key sent in the Full EKT Tag.
